adaptation_action: The project used climate modeling to predict which invasive plant species are likely to thrive under future weather conditions in specific areas. These models, combined with scientific analysis and community engagement, helped identify species that may become greater threats as the climate changes. At the same time, the team reviewed existing regulatory frameworks to pinpoint gaps or inconsistencies that might allow harmful species to go unaddressed. They also worked closely with a range of stakeholders—including land managers, researchers, and government officials—through workshops and discussions to ensure proposed strategies were grounded in practical realities. This interdisciplinary and participatory approach enabled the project to develop recommendations that were both scientifically informed and realistically implementable.

limitations: The source reports project information, but this record does not establish that the same outcomes will occur in other places or under different conditions.
outcomes: The project produced a prioritized list of invasive species expected to pose future threats due to climate change, which can help guide prevention and early detection efforts. The team also offered policy recommendations aimed at strengthening regulatory tools, especially around pathways like horticultural trade and transportation where new invasions are most likely. In addition, they developed user-friendly decision-support tools to help land managers incorporate climate and invasive species data into their planning. Moreover, the project fostered a more proactive mindset among stakeholders, emphasizing the need to anticipate and prevent invasions rather than react after damage has already been done.

summary: The primary goal of the Northwest RISCC Network project was to assess and address how climate change may increase the risk posed by invasive plant species in the Pacific Northwest. As temperatures rise and ecosystems shift, some non-native species that were previously benign or regionally constrained may become invasive threats. The project aimed to help land managers, policymakers, and regulatory agencies prepare for these changes by identifying high-risk species and adapting management tools and regulations accordingly.
title: Risks & Regulation of Invasive Plants in a Changing Climate
transferability: Using climate-informed modeling to anticipate future invasion risks is an example of how Washington can integrate climate science into natural resource planning and decision-making. It also highlights ways Washington can build resilient ecological systems by assessing and addressing vulnerabilities early.
